TFN Content Studio — Installation, Startup and Usage Manual

Version of 2026-10-03. For the design background see PLAN.md; for a short overview see README.md.

Just want to read this, with nothing set up? Open MANUAL.html (in the same folder as this file) in any browser — it is one self-contained file that needs no studio, Python or internet. The running studio serves the same page at /manual; every page's top bar has a Manual ↗ link to it, and ./bin/tfn-studio manual prints its location.

What this is. A small web app that runs on your own computer. You design quests, camps (props + creatures + spawn markers), spawn groups and encounter blueprints on a map or in forms. The studio turns that into the exact files The Frozen North (TFN) expects (src/**/*.json, a few .nss), shows you the diff, validates it, and only then — when you press Apply — writes it into your TFN checkout. Everything can be undone.

1. Quick start#

Open a terminal in the studio folder and run:

cd ~/git/Q-tfn-content-studio
./bin/tfn-studio doctor                       # checks Python, your TFN checkout, tools, NWN install, port

doctor prints one line per check: [ok], [warn] (optional feature reduced) or [FAIL] (must fix).

If it says the TFN checkout is missing — this is the error ... does not look like a TFN checkout (missing src/git or src/are) — tell the studio where your checkout really is. The default is ~/git/the-frozen-north; if yours lives anywhere else, use one of:

./bin/tfn-studio --tfn "/path/to/the-frozen-north" doctor       # one-off (works before OR after the command)
export TFN_ROOT="/path/to/the-frozen-north"                     # for this terminal
echo 'export TFN_ROOT="/path/to/the-frozen-north"' >> ~/.zshrc  # permanently (macOS default shell: zsh)

The right folder is the nasher project root — the folder that directly contains src/, nasher.cfg and tools/ (so that src/are and src/git exist inside it). Pointing at src/ itself, or at the folder above the checkout, does not work.

When doctor is green (warnings are fine):

./bin/tfn-studio serve --open                 # opens http://127.0.0.1:8350/ in your browser

Stop it with Ctrl+C.

2. Requirements#

NeedDetails
Python 3.9 or newerNothing to pip install — the studio uses only the standard library. macOS's stock /usr/bin/python3 (3.9.x, from the Xcode Command Line Tools) works; so does Homebrew Python. Tested on 3.9 and 3.10.
gitUsed to show the branch and to refuse overwriting files you have uncommitted changes in. macOS: xcode-select --install.
A TFN checkoutThe nasher project (the-frozen-north) with src/are, src/git, src/utc, src/dlg, … The studio reads and (on Apply) writes only inside its src/ folder.
A modern browserCurrent Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari. No internet needed: all pages and scripts are local.
NWN tools (recommended)nwn_gff (JSON round-trip validation), nwnsc (script compile check). TFN ships them in its own tools/<platform>/ folder, so with a normal checkout they are found automatically. Without them validation of that kind is skipped (shown as info).
NWN:EE install (optional)Gives exact ground heights and a walkable/non-walkable overlay on the map (needs data/nwn_base.key and the nwn_resman_extract tool). Without it, heights are guessed from neighbouring objects and there is no walkability check.

Tool folders are named per operating system: linux, macos_arm64 (Apple-silicon Macs), win. On an Intel Mac no bundled tools exist; set NWN_GFF / NWNSC to your own builds, or live with the skipped checks.

3. Installation#

3.1 Recommended folder layout#

Keep the three things side by side:

~/git/
  the-frozen-north/        your TFN checkout (has src/, tools/, nwn-base-scripts/, nasher.cfg)
  Q-tfn-content-studio/    this tool
  nwn-tools/               OPTIONAL shared tools: macos_arm64/…, linux/…, win/…  (only needed if TFN's own tools/ is missing)

Nothing is installed system-wide; the studio runs from its folder.

3.2 Getting the studio onto the machine#

You need the Q-tfn-content-studio folder (about 65 files, under 1 MB). Pick whichever fits:

  • Through git (recommended — later updates are just git pull). The studio's repository is a bare repo on the Linux machine, /var/www/storage/git/q-tfn-content-studio (the origin remote of its working copy). On the machine you want it on, clone it over SSH (replace user@host with how you log in to the machine that holds /var/www/storage): git clone user@host:/var/www/storage/git/q-tfn-content-studio ~/git/Q-tfn-content-studio.
  • Copy it from the machine it was built on (replace user/host): rsync -av --exclude .studio --exclude __pycache__ --exclude .git user@host:git/Q-tfn-content-studio/ ~/git/Q-tfn-content-studio/
  • From an archive: unpack the .tar.gz you were sent into ~/git/ (tar -xzf Q-tfn-content-studio.tar.gz -C ~/git).

Make sure the launcher is executable: chmod +x ~/git/Q-tfn-content-studio/bin/tfn-studio (or always start it as python3 bin/tfn-studio …).

3.3 Check Python#

python3 --version        # 3.9 or newer

If macOS answers with a dialog about "command line developer tools", accept it (that installs python3 and git), or run xcode-select --install, or brew install python.

3.4 Tell the studio where TFN is#

Default location: ~/git/the-frozen-north. Anything else: --tfn PATH or TFN_ROOT (see Quick start). Check the folder is right:

ls "/path/to/the-frozen-north/src" | head        # should list: are  dlg  git  jrl  nss  utc  utp …
ls "/path/to/the-frozen-north/src/are" | head -3

If src/are is empty or missing, that clone is incomplete (or is on a branch without content): git -C … status, git -C … pull.

3.5 Tools (nwn_gff, nwnsc, nwn_resman_extract)#

The studio looks, in this order, for each tool:

  1. an environment variable naming the program: NWN_GFF, NWNSC, NASHER, NWN_RESMAN_EXTRACT;
  2. $NWN_TOOLS/<platform>/… if you set NWN_TOOLS;
  3. <TFN>/tools/<platform>/… — TFN's own bundled tools;
  4. <TFN>/../nwn-tools/<platform>/… — a shared nwn-tools folder next to the checkout;
  5. <studio>/../nwn-tools/<platform>/….

<platform> is macos_arm64 on a Mac, linux on Linux, win on Windows. Inside it the programs are neverwinter/nwn_gff, neverwinter/nwn_resman_extract, nwnsc/nwnsc, nasher/nasher (Windows: .exe, and neverwinter64/).

macOS Gatekeeper. If a tool was copied through a browser, AirDrop or a zip, macOS may refuse to run it ("cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified"). Clear the quarantine flag once:

xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine ~/git/the-frozen-north/tools
chmod +x ~/git/the-frozen-north/tools/macos_arm64/*/*

3.6 NWN install (optional, for exact heights and walkability)#

The studio finds your NWN:EE install by itself if it is at one of the usual places (the folder must contain data/nwn_base.key):

OSChecked locations
any~/nwn-data
macOS~/Library/Application Support/Steam/steamapps/common/Neverwinter Nights
Linux~/.local/share/Steam/steamapps/common/Neverwinter Nights, ~/.steam/steam/steamapps/common/Neverwinter Nights
WindowsC:/Program Files (x86)/Steam/steamapps/common/Neverwinter Nights (and Program Files), C:/GOG Games/Neverwinter Nights Enhanced Edition

Elsewhere: export NWN_ROOT="/path/to/Neverwinter Nights" (the folder that contains data/). The optional user folder is taken from NWN_USER, else <install>/user, ~/Documents/Neverwinter Nights or ~/.local/share/Neverwinter Nights — whichever exists. TFN uses no haks and no custom TLK, so the base game is all that is needed.

3.7 Run the check#

./bin/tfn-studio doctor

Example of a healthy result (your versions and paths will differ):

[ok]   Python 3.9.6
[info] Darwin 24.5.0 (arm64); tool folder expected: macos_arm64
[ok]   Studio folder: /Users/sean/git/Q-tfn-content-studio
[ok]   git version 2.39.5
[ok]   TFN checkout: /Users/sean/git/the-frozen-north
[ok]   branch master, 0 uncommitted file(s)
[ok]   nwn_gff: /Users/sean/git/the-frozen-north/tools/macos_arm64/neverwinter/nwn_gff
[ok]   nwnsc: …/tools/macos_arm64/nwnsc/nwnsc
[ok]   NWN install: /Users/sean/Library/Application Support/Steam/steamapps/common/Neverwinter Nights
[ok]   port 8350 is free
Everything looks good. Start with:  ./bin/tfn-studio serve

A [warn] never stops the studio from running; it tells you which optional feature is reduced and how to enable it.

3.8 Optional: prove it works without touching TFN#

Staging only writes to the studio's own .studio/ folder, never to TFN:

./bin/tfn-studio quest describe q_example_wolves      # prints the 4-stage plan of the shipped example quest
./bin/tfn-studio quest stage q_example_wolves         # builds a change set + validates; prints its id
./bin/tfn-studio changes list
./bin/tfn-studio changes discard <id>                 # throw it away again

4. Starting and stopping#

cd ~/git/Q-tfn-content-studio
./bin/tfn-studio serve                 # http://127.0.0.1:8350/
OptionMeaning
--openopen the Dashboard in your default browser
--port Nuse another port (default 8350). If it is busy you get a clear error and a suggested port
--host Hbind address (default 127.0.0.1). Leave it. The studio has no login; see Safety
--tfn PATHwhich TFN checkout (also TFN_ROOT)
  • First start: the studio builds its content index in the background (the Dashboard shows building… …). On a fresh checkout that takes tens of seconds; afterwards only changed files are re-read (cache in .studio/cache/, safe to delete). You can already use the pages while it builds; lists fill in as soon as it is ready.
  • Open the address http://127.0.0.1:8350/ (or http://localhost:8350/). Other host names or your LAN address are refused on purpose.
  • Stop: Ctrl+C in the terminal. Staged change sets and undo records survive restarts.
  • Keep it running in the background: nohup ./bin/tfn-studio serve > /tmp/tfn-studio.log 2>&1 & (stop with kill <pid>), or use a second terminal tab.
  • Several checkouts / branches: run one studio per checkout on different ports, e.g. --tfn ~/git/tfn-a --port 8350 and --tfn ~/git/tfn-b --port 8351. Staged change sets are stored per studio folder, so apply each one against the checkout it was staged for.

The top bar of every page shows the TFN branch and path so you always know what you are editing, and a Manual ↗ link that opens this manual (at the section for the page you are on) in a new tab.

5. How you work with it (the loop)#

 design  →  Stage  →  review on Changes  →  Apply  →  build module  →  restart server  →  test in game
 (map / forms)  (nothing written to TFN yet)   (files written, undo kept)
  1. Design in Camp Builder, Spawn Designer or Quest Builder.
  2. Stage changes. The studio generates the files and validates them. The result is a change set; TFN is untouched.
  3. Review it on the Changes page: file list, coloured diffs, validation messages.
  4. Apply to TFN… writes the files into <TFN>/src/. Undo apply restores the previous files.
  5. Build and restart the module the way you normally do (section 11). area_init reads spawn markers, area variables and quest NPCs at module load, so a restart is required.
  6. Test in game.

Camps, spawn groups and quests need no database reseed (SEED_SYSTEM.md §12). New areas, tile edits, transitions and new item blueprints do.

Good habit: before the first Apply of a session, create a git branch in the TFN checkout (git -C ~/git/the-frozen-north switch -c content/my-new-camp) so all generated changes land on a branch you can review and merge.

6. Dashboard#

/ — status at a glance.

  • TFN checkout: path, branch @ commit, and the number of uncommitted files (Apply refuses to overwrite those).
  • Tools: nwn_gff, nwnsc, nasher — found (with path) or missing; walkmesh: game data found or unavailable.
  • Content: file counts per type (.are, .utc, .utp, .ute, .uti, .dlg); Index status and a Refresh index button (use it after you changed TFN files outside the studio, e.g. after a git pull).
  • Change sets: the latest staged/applied sets (click one to open it on the Changes page).
  • After you apply: the short reminder list from section 11.

Three big cards link to the builders; a fourth opens this manual.

7. Camp Builder#

/camps — place props, creatures, spawn markers and event waypoints on a map of an area, wire up spawn groups, stage. It can also build a random camp: a camp that the area creates only now and then, at one of several spots you choose (7.5).

7.1 Layout#

  • Left: Area (search and pick), Camp plan (title, id, cr, save/load), Place tabs.
  • Centre: the map. Top toolbar, then the canvas.
  • Right: Spawn groups, Events, Random camp, Plan objects (selection details), Stage.

7.2 Step by step#

  1. Pick an area. Search by name or resref (e.g. mantle) and click it. The card shows size, tileset, interior/exterior, the area's cr, how many creatures/props exist, and the spawn groups it already has. Changing area discards the current plan (it asks first).
  2. Name the plan. Title (e.g. "Wolf den in Mantle Clearing") — the Plan id is derived (a-z 0-9 _). Re-staging a plan with the same id replaces its objects instead of duplicating them. Set Area cr if the area has none (spawns/loot/XP need it; the card warns "no cr set").
  3. Place things with the tabs under Place:
    • Prefabs — ready-made layouts (bandit camp, goblin camp, hunter camp, wagon camp, ruined camp, tents, small camp, graveyard, spider nest, ambush site). Click one, then click the map to stamp it. R / Shift+R rotates before you click. If the prefab contains spawn markers, a box lets you map each prefab group to a group number of this area (pick an unused one for a dedicated camp group). Find open ground jumps the view to the nearest place where the whole footprint is walkable (needs the NWN install) and offers a Stamp "…" here button.
    • Props — every placeable TFN already uses (searchable; filters: decor, container, light, usable, respawning). Containers roll TFN loot (treas_*) — place them deliberately. plx_ props respawn on every area refresh.
    • Creatures — TFN's creatures plus base-game ones TFN areas already place (filters: monster, npc, other, henchman, base-game). A hand-placed creature is recorded by area_init and respawns at that exact spot every refresh. For roaming groups use Spawns.
    • Spawns — invisible spawn markers for group 1–9. area_init reads each marker's position and removes it; the group's encounter is spread over all its markers (more markers = better spread).
    • Waypoints — event waypoints (_wp_event). On each refresh there is an event_chance% roll; on success one event script runs with a random event waypoint as the acting object.
  4. Spawn groups (right). + group adds a row: choose the encounter blueprint (.ute), the number of spawns and an optional spawn script. + new encounter… opens a small encounter editor and adds the new .ute to the same change set. Markers in the plan whose group has no encounter are flagged ("nothing will spawn there").
  5. Events (right). + event adds script names (event1…event9 on the area); set event_chance %.
  6. Adjust. Click an object (Select tool, Esc) to see it under Plan objects: x, y, z (leave empty for the exact walkmesh height), facing, ⟲/⟳ 15°, duplicate, delete, group (markers), tag. Prefab stamps can be selected/rotated/deleted as a whole ("select all", "⟳ stamp", "delete stamp").
  7. Save the plan (Save plan) any time → specs/camps/<id>.json; the dropdown reloads saved plans. Your own layout can become a prefab: Save as prefab… → prefabs/<id>.json.
  8. Stage changes (right, bottom). The button is disabled while something blocking is missing (no area, no id, a group without encounter, nothing placed). Warnings (no cr, markers without encounter) do not block. After staging, Review & apply → opens the change set.

7.3 Map controls#

ActionHow
Zoommouse wheel / two-finger scroll
Panhold Space and drag (works on trackpads), or right-button drag
Fit area to viewF or the Fit button
Select / cancel a toolEsc
Rotate placement (or selection) ±15°R / Shift+R (or the ⟲ ⟳ buttons)
Nudge selectionarrow keys 0.5 m; with Shift 2 m
Delete selectionDelete or Backspace
UndoCtrl+Z (⌘Z on macOS)
Place without grid snaphold Alt (⌥ on macOS)
Move / turn / delete a camp spotSelect tool: click a spot (a teal numbered circle) and drag it; R / Shift+R turns it; Delete removes it
Layerscheckboxes: tiles, walkable, grid, existing objects, camp spots, labels; snap 0.5 m

Coordinates are metres: x east, y north, origin at the south-west corner, 10 m per tile. Facing is in degrees, 0 = east, 90 = north. Colours: creatures red, props blue, waypoints green, doors orange, triggers purple, spawn markers magenta, random-camp spots teal.

7.4 Heights and walkability#

With the NWN install available, every new object gets its exact Z from the tile walkmesh (calibrated: 99 % of TFN's existing objects match within 0.35 m), the walkable layer is shown, and creatures, spawn markers and waypoints placed on non-walkable ground get a red ring and a warning. Props on non-walkable surfaces (rocks, trees, walls) are allowed and only noted. Without the install, Z is guessed from neighbours — check heights in the toolset.

7.5 Random camp: a camp that appears only sometimes#

Everything you place normally is permanent: it is written into the area and is there after every refresh. A random camp is different. The props and creatures of the plan become a template, and the area builds that template only now and then, when it refreshes, at one of the spots you chose — each spot with its own direction, so tents, fire and guards line up with the terrain wherever the camp turns up. Nothing of the camp is stored in the area file.

How it works in the game. When an area refreshes TFN makes one roll against the area's event_chance (most TFN areas use 20 %; 50 % when none is set). If the roll succeeds, one of the area's event scripts (event1…event9) runs. The studio writes such an event script for your camp, so the camp shares that roll with the area's other events (for example wandering adventurers): chance the camp appears = event_chance × the camp's event slots ÷ all event slots. The camp is removed again with the rest of the area's spawns at the next refresh.

  1. Build the camp as usual — place the props and creatures (or stamp a prefab) where you like; this is only the design. Spawn markers and waypoints you place stay permanent, ordinary area objects.
  2. In Random camp (right) tick Build this camp only sometimes, at a random spot.
  3. Add spots. Press + Spot (click map) and click the map: the whole camp follows the cursor, turned by the toolbar rotation (R rotates it). Each spot is a numbered teal circle whose arrow shows the way the camp's front faces, with the camp drawn half-transparent at every spot (red marks warn about objects on non-walkable ground or outside the area). Drag a spot to move it, type exact x / y / ° in the list, turn it with ⟲ ⟳ (45°). Suggest adds spots on open ground where the whole camp fits and nothing existing is in the way (needs the NWN install); press it again for different spots. Import markers takes waypoints that are already in the area: its _wp_event event waypoints and any waypoint whose tag starts with camp_spot — place those in the toolset where you want the camp, and rotate them the way the camp should face (a waypoint's facing becomes the spot's direction).
  4. Direction. Design the camp with its "front" pointing north (90°). The pivot (default: the centre of the camp; Set… moves it) is the point that lands on each spot; a spot turns the camp about the pivot by (spot direction − 90°). Facing is in degrees, 0 = east, 90 = north.
  5. Also build it where it is designed now adds the design location as one more possible place. With no spots at all the design location is the only place.
  6. Replaces (optional) — choose one of the area's spawn groups (random1…9). While the camp stands, that group's creatures are removed as they spawn: all of them, or only those within m metres of the camp. When the camp is not built the group spawns as usual, and a spawn script the group already had keeps running. One camp can replace a group; two camps cannot replace the same one.
  7. Event slots (1–4): a camp that takes more slots is picked more often (TFN itself lists eve_adventure twice in some areas for the same reason).
  8. Look at the info card: it shows the chance per refresh (and per spot), which event slots are used, which other events share the roll, a _wp_event waypoint the studio will add when the area has none (events only run from one), and every problem per spot. Errors (a spot that pushes the camp out of the area) block Stage changes; warnings do not.
  9. Stage, review, Apply, build the module and restart the server like any other change.

What gets written. src/nss/eve_<plan id>.nss (the event script; the name can be changed — at most 16 characters) and, when it replaces a group, src/nss/spw_<…>.nss (the gate script); the area's eventN variables and, for a replaced group, its randomN_spawn_script. Both scripts begin with a header comment (// tfn-studio camp event: plan <id>). Only scripts with that header are ever overwritten — a name that belongs to TFN or to another plan is refused. Staging the same plan again replaces the scripts; turning random camp off removes the wiring again and the props and creatures become permanent area objects like any other plan.

Good to know.

  • Every spot is checked when you stage: heights come from the tile walkmesh object by object, creatures on non-walkable ground and objects too close to existing ones give warnings, a camp that would reach outside the area is an error. Without the NWN install the camp stands at one guessed height per spot and the card says so.
  • The camp's props behave like toolset-placed ones: containers, trapped props and props with an inventory become static decor, treas_* props roll TFN loot, plx_ props stay as they are; creatures with a quest are registered as quest NPCs.
  • TFN counts an area's events from event1 up to the first empty slot, so the studio keeps the slots contiguous (and the Changes page warns about an existing gap that hides events). An area can have at most nine event slots; a camp can have at most 24 spots.
  • Adding a camp to an area that already has events makes those events a little rarer, because they share the roll — the info card lists them. If the area has no event_chance, TFN uses 50 % for all events: set it under Events.
  • To see the camp in game quickly, stage it with event_chance 100 and Event slots 4 while testing, then put the real values back and stage again.

8. Spawn Designer#

/spawns — author encounter blueprints (.ute). In TFN a .ute is the data container behind a random spawn group (random1…random9 on an area): a pool of common creatures, an optional pool of unique creatures, a difficulty and an optional rare spawn.

  • Left: all existing blueprints (search; creature count and number of areas using each), + New encounter, and your saved drafts.
  • Editor (centre):
    • Resref (≤16 chars, a-z 0-9 _; the badge says new / editing existing / invalid) and optional Name.
    • Difficulty (unique chance): Very easy 5 % · Easy 10 % · Normal 15 % · Hard 20 % · Impossible 25 % — the chance that a spawn is taken from the unique pool.
    • Rare creature (15 % per refresh): optional creature resref.
    • Creatures: add from the searchable list; each is common or unique (single spawn).
    • Preview: pick a Group spawns number and optionally an area to Check CR against. You see the expected number of each creature per refresh, the spawn range, the average common CR, and warnings/advice (for example CR outliers for that area).
  • Right: Used by — areas/groups/spawn counts/CR where this blueprint is used (links open the Camp Builder on that area). Editing an existing blueprint rewrites its creature list, difficulty and rare entry; other fields are kept.
  • Stage changes validates and creates the change set; Save draft keeps the form in specs/utes/.

9. Quest Builder#

/quests — multi-stage quests built the way TFN's inc_quest.nss expects: a journal entry per stage, and variables on NPCs, creatures, items and areas that advance the stage.

9.1 Layout#

  • Left: + New quest, Your drafts (saved specs), and Existing TFN quests (search; click for a read-only view of how a real quest is wired).
  • Centre: basics, Quest giver, Stages.
  • Right: Mechanism plan (live summary: stage → mechanism → reward), Stage changes, Save draft.

9.2 Step by step#

  1. Basics. Journal tag q_… for a quest or b_… for a bounty (bounties can be redone every 6 h); at most 27 characters. The chip says ok, invalid, or tag used by a TFN quest. Quest name, Journal priority 0–4.

  2. Quest giver.

    • Create a new NPC (clone an existing one): new resref, display name, Clone appearance & stats from (pick from the list), a greeting for when no quest applies.
    • Use an existing NPC: the quest variables are added to the blueprint and every placed instance, and the quest nodes are merged into the NPC's existing conversation (or a new dialog is created).
    • Optionally place the NPC in an area (Pick on map… shows a map; spots near existing creatures are known to be walkable).

  3. Stages. Stage 1 is always the giver's offer (offer text, accept/decline replies and NPC answers). Add more with the buttons:

    • + Talk to an NPC — the player returns to the giver (or another existing NPC) and the quest advances.
    • + Kill a creature — a new named boss (clone of a creature, optionally placed in an area) or an existing creature blueprint; tick boss for better loot / XP / treasure-map chance.
    • + Pick up an item — a new quest item (resref, name, description) dropped by a chosen creature.
    • + Enter an area — advances when the player enters an area (a tiny generic enter_quest_adv script is generated for you).

    Every stage has its journal text. Reorder with ↑ ↓, Remove where allowed. The last stage completes the quest and is where the reward goes: XP tier (1–4 = 50/100/200/400 base XP), for level, gold, item.

  4. Check the Mechanism plan (right) — it lists, per stage, which NPC/creature/item/area carries which variable.

  5. Save draft any time (specs/quests/<tag>.json). Stage changes generates the journal category (appended to src/jrl/module.jrl.json), dialog, blueprints, items, variables and placements, then validates everything.

Existing NPC dialogs are never overwritten: the quest nodes are merged in and tagged so re-staging replaces them cleanly.

9.3 Script style: Modern or Older (top-right button)#

The button at the top right of the Quest Builder page — Quest scripts: Modern ⇄ / Quest scripts: Older ⇄ — chooses how the quest's conversation is wired. Click it to switch; the choice is saved with the draft ("script_style": "modern" or "legacy" in the spec).

  • Modern (the default for every new quest). One generic script does each kind of check, and the conversation hands it a small note — a parameter — saying which quest slot to look at. "Is the player currently at this stage?" is always dlg_q_chk_at with the note target = 3, whatever the slot. There is no slot limit below the game's own (19), and no pile of near-identical scripts.
  • Older. What the studio did before: it calls TFN's slot-numbered scripts, one per slot (dlg_q_chk_atc1, dlg_q_chk_atc2, … up to 9; above 9 it falls back to dlg_q_chk_multi). Use it only when you want a new quest to look exactly like TFN's older ones.
  • Your existing quests are never converted. A saved draft that has no script_style (everything made before this feature, including the shipped example) opens as Older and produces exactly the same output as before. Switching a draft's style and staging it again simply regenerates its dialog nodes in the other style.

What is a "parameter"?#

A dialog line can run a script, and the dialog editor lets you attach little Key = Value notes to that line. The script reads them while it runs. So instead of writing a new script for every quest slot, you write one script and say, on each dialog line, which slot (target = 3) it should use. Nothing about the quest changes for the player; only the bookkeeping behind the conversation is simpler.

How a quest conversation works (plain English)#

Every quest NPC carries slots: little labelled notes on the NPC named quest1, quest2, … Each note says "I am the person who moves quest Wolf Hunt to stage 05" (stored as 05_q_wolf_hunt), and may carry a reward. The conversation then follows the same story every time you talk to the NPC:

  1. You speak to the NPC. The game looks down the dialog's starting list from the top and uses the first line whose condition says yes.
  2. "Can I hand you the next stage?" (dlg_q_chk_eli, target = slot). It looks at the slot's note and asks: is the player one stage behind the stage this slot advances to, and have all required earlier stages been done? If yes, this is a turn-in line ("Splendid, here is your pay"). The studio puts the latest stages first so a player who finished everything is not offered the beginning again.
  3. "Are you in the middle of this stage?" (dlg_q_chk_at, target = slot — the Older style uses dlg_q_chk_atcN). If the player is exactly at the stage this slot handed out, the NPC gives a reminder ("Have you finished yet?") — or a farewell if it was the last stage.
  4. "Is this a brand-new player?" The stage-1 offer uses the same "can I hand you the next stage" check, so only players who haven't started see the offer.
  5. Nobody matched? A new NPC falls back to its plain greeting.
  6. The player picks a reply. When a line that advances is spoken (accepting the offer, or the turn-in text), it runs dlg_q_adv with target = slot. That script re-checks the rules, moves the journal to the new stage, and gives the slot's reward (XP, gold, item).
  7. Other mechanisms (kill, pick up, enter an area) use the very same slot notes, but placed on the creature, item or area instead of the NPC; no dialog is needed for those.

In short: the notes on the object say what a stage is; the parameter on each dialog line says which note to read; three generic scripts do the work.

Question the dialog asksModernOlder
Can the player be handed the next stage?dlg_q_chk_eli + target=Ksame
Advance the quest nowdlg_q_adv + target=Ksame
Is the player currently at this stage?dlg_q_chk_at + target=K (any slot)dlg_q_chk_atcK (slots 1–9), else dlg_q_chk_multi

The only script the studio adds to TFN for this is dlg_q_chk_at (shown on the Changes page the first time a Modern quest is staged, and skipped if it is already there).

9.4 Limits#

LimitValueNotes
Quests in the moduleno fixed capeach quest is one journal category
Quest slots on one NPC, item or area19 (quest1 … quest19)TFN's HIGHEST_QUEST_COUNT = 20; area_init.nss repeats the number. The studio uses the next free slot automatically
Prerequisites per stage19same constant
Stages per quest99two-digit stage prefix (NN_tag)
Quest tag length27 charactersq_… or b_…

Raising the slot limit would mean editing TFN's inc_quest.nss and the hard-coded number in area_init.nss; the studio does not do this for you.

9.5 Converting older quests to parameters (optional, never automatic)#

TFN's older dialogs (86 of them today) call numbered scripts such as dlg_q_adv3. A command can rewrite them to the modern form (dlg_q_adv + target=3). It only ever runs when you ask, and it only stages a change set — nothing in TFN changes until you review and apply it, and Undo restores it.

./bin/tfn-studio quest convert --check            # dry run: lists what would change, writes nothing
./bin/tfn-studio quest convert --dialog aarin     # stage ONE dialog first and look at its diff
./bin/tfn-studio quest convert                    # stage them all

What keeps it safe:

  • It changes only the script name and its parameter list on a dialog line — never text, links or order.
  • A line that already has parameters (for example an area-effect advance, or a check with an npc_tag) is left alone and listed.
  • Before converting, it confirms that each numbered script really is "the generic script with the slot filled in"; any family that is not is left untouched.
  • Per dialog it checks that the list of (script, slot) calls is identical before and after, and that the file round-trips byte for byte; otherwise the dialog is skipped.
  • The numbered scripts are not deleted; other content may still call them.

Risk: low-to-moderate. The rewrite is mechanical and checked, but only a playthrough proves a quest still behaves. Convert one NPC, restart, test its quests, then do the rest.

10. Changes: review, apply, undo#

/changes — every staged set, newest first, with staged or applied chips.

For the selected set you see:

  • Files — new / edit, +added −removed lines and a note; click a file for its coloured diff.

  • Notes — important facts (e.g. "Restart the server after applying…").

  • Validation — runs automatically and with Re-validate:

    1. canonical JSON formatting (byte-identical to what nwn_gff writes, so diffs only show real changes);
    2. structure and cross-reference checks (blueprints exist, group markers exist, cr set, quest tag length and journal entries, dialog graph integrity, scripts exist, …);
    3. a real nwn_gff JSON → GFF → JSON round trip (proves the toolset/engine can load the files);
    4. nwnsc compile of every generated script (with a time limit — nwnsc can hang on some syntax errors).

    Messages are error (blocks Apply unless forced), warning, or info (including "SKIP: tool not found"). Problems that were already in a file before your change are listed as (pre-existing) warnings and do not block.

  • Apply to TFN… → confirm. Apply refuses files that have uncommitted git changes (you may choose Apply anyway) and files that changed since you staged (stage again). It writes only inside <TFN>/src/ and keeps an undo record.

  • Undo apply restores the files exactly as they were before.

  • Discard deletes the staged set (applied files are not touched).

11. After Apply: build, restart, test#

Apply only changes source files. To see the result in game, build and run the module as usual. TFN documents these routes (see TFN's docs/TEST_PLAN.md, CHANGES_AND_TEST_PLAN.md, BUGFIX_TESTING.md):

  • Pack only (routine rebuild; does not touch databases) — nasher from TFN's bundled tools, e.g. on Linux: 
    cd ~/git/the-frozen-north
./tools/linux/nasher/nasher pack -y \
  --erfUtil:"$PWD/tools/linux/neverwinter/nwn_erf" --gffUtil:"$PWD/tools/linux/neverwinter/nwn_gff" \
  --tlkUtil:"$PWD/tools/linux/neverwinter/nwn_tlk" --nssCompiler:"$PWD/tools/linux/nwnsc/nwnsc" \
  --nssFlags:"-lowqey -i $PWD/.build/include-shims -i $PWD/nwn-base-scripts"
    On a Mac use tools/macos_arm64/… (compare the flags in macos_nasher_install.sh; macOS file names are case-insensitive, so the include-shims folder is not needed). The result is .build/modules/TFN.mod.
  • Full install script (linux_nasher_install.sh / macos_nasher_install.sh / win_nasher_install.bat) additionally wipes and reseeds the campaign databases and deletes .build/modules — don't use it for a routine rebuild.
  • swamp users: from ~/git (not inside the TFN repo) swamp model method run thefrozennorth-build build.
  • Restart the dev server (./linux_run_server_dev.sh / ./macos_run_server_dev.sh / the win_ equivalent) or deploy the new TFN.mod to the server you test on.

In game:

  • Camps/spawns: the area's spawn refresh creates the group; hand-placed creatures and plx_ props reappear at their spots each refresh. See SPAWN_SYSTEM.md for timing, cr, markers and events.
  • Quests: talk to the giver, check the journal after each stage, finish the quest. Quest NPCs are registered at module load by area_init.
  • Check object heights if the NWN install was not available when you staged (Z was inferred from neighbours).

12. Command line reference#

Everything the web pages do is also available (and scriptable) from the terminal. --tfn PATH can be placed anywhere on the line.

CommandWhat it does
doctor [--port N]environment check (works even if the TFN checkout cannot be found)
manual [--open]print where MANUAL.html is (needs no checkout or tools); --open shows it in your browser
serve [--port N] [--host H] [--open]start the web UI
statuscheckout, branch, tools, counts, staged changes (JSON)
indexbuild/refresh the content indexes
areas [--filter TEXT] / area RESREF [--objects]list areas / show one area (spawn groups, cr, optionally every object)
prefabslist camp prefabs
camp stamp PLAN PREFAB --x X --y Y [--area A] [--title T] [--rotation DEG] [--cr N] [--group-map 1=4,2=5]create specs/camps/PLAN.json from a prefab
camp stamp PLAN PREFAB … --random-camp [--spot X,Y[,DEG] …] [--include-here] [--weight N] [--replaces-group N] [--replace-radius M] [--event-chance PCT] [--script NAME]stamp the prefab as a random camp: built at one of the --spot places (repeatable) when the area refreshes
camp spots PLAN [--count N] [--seed S] [--add]suggest open spots for a plan's random camp (needs the NWN install); --add appends them to the plan file
camp stage SPEC [--no-validate]build a change set from a camp plan (SPEC = name in specs/camps/ or a path)
ute stage SPEC [--no-validate]build a change set from an encounter spec (specs/utes/)
quest describe SPECprint the stage → mechanism plan
quest stage SPEC [--no-validate]build a change set from a quest spec (specs/quests/TAG.json)
quest convert [--check] [--dialog RESREF …] [--no-validate]convert older numbered quest scripts in dialogs to parameters (§9.5); --check = dry run, otherwise stages a change set
changes list / show ID [--diff] / validate IDinspect staged sets
changes apply ID [--allow-dirty] [--force]write a set into TFN (--allow-dirty: even if files have uncommitted changes; --force: despite validation errors/conflicts)
changes undo ID [--force] / changes discard IDrestore the files / delete the staged set
global --jsonmachine-readable output where supported

Typical scripted run:

./bin/tfn-studio camp stamp wolf_den hunter_camp --area mantle --x 70 --y 70 --rotation 30 --cr 4 --group-map 1=4
./bin/tfn-studio camp stage wolf_den
./bin/tfn-studio changes show <id> --diff | less
./bin/tfn-studio changes apply <id>

A random camp from the terminal (the camp appears at one of three places in mantle, turned the way each X,Y,DEGREES says — use your own spots, or let camp spots find them):

./bin/tfn-studio camp stamp hunters hunter_camp --area mantle --x 70 --y 70 --random-camp --spot 14.5,75.5,90 --spot 134.5,64.5,270 --spot 91.5,128.5,0
./bin/tfn-studio camp spots hunters --count 3 --add        # or let the studio find open ground for more spots
./bin/tfn-studio camp stage hunters

Specs are plain JSON, declarative and re-appliable. Shipped examples: specs/camps/example_bandit_camp.json, specs/camps/example_random_camp.json, specs/quests/q_example_wolves.json. A camp spec lists objects (kind: placeable / creature / marker / waypoint, resref, x, y, facing, optional z, tag, group), groups (n, ute, spawns, script), events, event_chance, cr, new_utes, and optionally camp_event (script, weight, origin {x, y, facing}, spots [{x, y, facing}], include_origin, replaces_group, replace_radius) to make its placeables and creatures a random camp. A quest spec lists tag, name, priority, giver, script_style (modern or legacy; absent = legacy, see §9.3), and stages (each with via: talk / kill / pickup / explore).

13. Where things live#

PathContents
<studio>/bin/tfn-studiothe launcher
<studio>/MANUAL.md, MANUAL.htmlthis manual: the Markdown source and the single-file browser version (after editing the Markdown run python3 scripts/build_manual.py to regenerate the HTML)
<studio>/specs/{camps,quests,utes}/your saved plans/drafts (commit these)
<studio>/prefabs/camp prefabs (10 shipped; Save as prefab… adds more)
<studio>/.studio/changes/<id>/staged change sets
<studio>/.studio/applied/<id>/undo records of applied sets
<studio>/.studio/cache/, .studio/gamedata/content index cache; tilesets/walkmeshes extracted from the NWN install (all safe to delete)
<TFN>/src/**only here does Apply write: git (area objects/variables), utc, utp, ute, uti, dlg, jrl/module.jrl.json, nss (the small generic scripts and the random-camp event/gate scripts)

What each builder generates:

  • Camps/spawns: props → Placeable List instances; creatures → Creature List instances (the blueprint's variables are copied, as the toolset does); spawn markers → creatures with resref random1…random9; area variables randomN, randomN_spawns, randomN_spawn_script, cr, eventN, event_chance; event waypoints (_wp_event); new encounters → src/ute/<resref>.ute.json. Every generated instance carries the local variable studio_plan = <plan id>.
  • Random camps: the props and creatures are not written to the area; instead src/nss/eve_<id>.nss (builds the camp at a random spot), optionally src/nss/spw_<…>.nss (removes a replaced spawn group's creatures while the camp stands), the area's eventN / randomN_spawn_script variables, and a _wp_event waypoint when the area has none.
  • Quests: journal category in src/jrl/module.jrl.json; giver blueprint (cloned, Plot=1) and dialog (TFN's generic dlg_q_chk_eli / dlg_q_adv scripts plus dlg_q_chk_at — or dlg_q_chk_atcN in the Older style, §9.3 — or merged into an existing dialog); questK = "NN_<tag>" plus questK_reward_* on the NPC (blueprint and placed instances), quest_kill on kill targets, a quest-tagged item for pickups, questK + enter_script on explore areas.

14. Safety model and good habits#

  • Generators write only to staging. Apply is the only step that touches TFN, and only inside <TFN>/src/.
  • Apply refuses files with uncommitted git changes and files changed since staging; every Apply keeps an undo record.
  • Names are validated (a-z 0-9 _, ≤16 chars for new resrefs). Existing dialogs are merged, not overwritten.
  • The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, checks the Host header, requires a per-run token and same-origin Origin on every change request, and sends no CORS headers. It has no login — never bind it to a LAN address or forward its port.
  • Generated scripts (random camps) carry a header naming their plan, and only scripts with that header are ever overwritten — TFN's own scripts, scripts of other plans and base-game script names are refused.
  • The studio never commits, pushes or builds anything.

Good habits: work on a git branch in TFN; keep TFN's working tree clean before Apply (so the dirty-guard stays useful); commit after each Apply so each studio change is one reviewable commit; keep your specs/ and prefabs/ in the studio repo; rebuild and restart before judging a change in game.

15. Troubleshooting#

SymptomCause and fix
error: … is not a TFN checkout (older versions: … does not look like a TFN checkout (missing src/git or src/are))The path the studio used has no src/git and src/are. It says where the path came from (--tfn, TFN_ROOT or the default ~/git/the-frozen-north) and suggests nearby checkouts. Fix: ./bin/tfn-studio --tfn "/real/path" … or export TFN_ROOT=… (see Quick start). Check with ls /real/path/src/are | head -3. ./bin/tfn-studio doctor shows everything at once.
permission denied: ./bin/tfn-studiochmod +x bin/tfn-studio, or run python3 bin/tfn-studio ….
python3: command not found / developer-tools dialogxcode-select --install or brew install python.
tfn-studio needs Python 3.9 or newerInstall a newer Python and start with that: python3.12 bin/tfn-studio serve.
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for | on Python 3.9You have a copy from before 2026-10-02. Update the studio (section 17).
cannot listen on 127.0.0.1:8350 … Is another studio already running?Stop the other one (Ctrl+C in its terminal) or use --port 8351.
Browser shows forbidden / the page does not loadUse exactly http://127.0.0.1:PORT/ (or localhost). Host names, LAN addresses and tunnels are refused on purpose.
Dashboard: tool missing; validation says SKIP: … not foundSee 3.5. Check ./bin/tfn-studio doctor; set NWN_TOOLS or NWN_GFF / NWNSC.
SKIP: … cannot run on this machineThe tool is for another OS/CPU (e.g. Linux or Apple-silicon binary on an Intel Mac). Point NWN_GFF / NWNSC at a build for your machine.
macOS: "nwn_gff" cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verifiedxattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <TFN>/tools and chmod +x <TFN>/tools/macos_arm64/*/*.
Dashboard: walkmesh unavailable; no walkable overlayNWN install not found. export NWN_ROOT="…/Neverwinter Nights" (the folder containing data/nwn_base.key) and make sure nwn_resman_extract is found. Delete .studio/gamedata/ if you changed installs.
Index stuck on building… or shows an errorPress Refresh index; if it persists delete .studio/cache/ and restart. Check the terminal for the Python error.
Lists (areas, creatures, props) are emptyThe index is still building, or the checkout is incomplete (src/utc, src/utp missing → doctor warns).
Apply refused: uncommitted changesCommit or stash your changes in those TFN files, or choose Apply anyway if you accept mixing them with generated edits.
Apply refused: changed since stagingA file was edited after you staged. Stage again.
Validation error: round trip / TemplateResRef does not match file name / missing blueprintRead the message — it names the file. Usually a typo in a resref or a blueprint that is not in TFN. Fix in the builder and stage again (re-staging replaces the old set's output).
compiler timed outnwnsc hangs on some syntax errors; the studio gives up after 30 s. Check the generated script for typos (only the tiny generic enter-script is generated).
Nothing changed in gameThe module was not rebuilt/redeployed, or the server was not restarted (area_init runs at module load). Spawns also need a cr on the area.
Random camp never shows upIt is a chance (see the info card: often 5 % or less per refresh). Events also need a _wp_event waypoint in the area and the area's event list must have no gap (the Changes page warns about both). Test with event_chance 100 and 4 event slots, then restore them.
Random camp: not enough free event slotsThe area already uses all nine eventN slots. Remove or merge one of its events, or lower the camp's Event slots.
Random camp: … already exists and belongs to another tool or planThe script name is taken by a script the studio did not generate for this plan. Pick another name under Event script.
Random camp: objects would fall outside the areaA spot is too close to the edge for the camp's size (or turned so that it sticks out). Move the spot inwards or use Suggest.
Camp objects float or sinkHeights were inferred (no NWN install). Install/point NWN_ROOT, restage; or fix heights in the toolset.
Quest giver does not reactQuest NPCs must exist at module load; restart the server. Existing NPC? Make sure its conversation was merged (see the file list on the Changes page).
"Staged, but validation found errors" toastThe set exists but has errors; open Changes, read them, fix, stage again.

If something else goes wrong, run ./bin/tfn-studio doctor and look at the terminal where serve is running — Python errors appear there.

17. Updating, moving and removing#

  • Update: replace the studio folder's code with the newer version (same methods as 3.2), keeping your specs/, prefabs/ and .studio/ if you want to keep drafts and staged sets. With git: git pull. Then ./bin/tfn-studio doctor.
  • Move to another computer: copy the folder (without .studio/ unless you need the staged sets) and install the TFN checkout there; run doctor.
  • Remove: delete the studio folder. Nothing is installed elsewhere; TFN is never modified except by Apply (undo any applied set from its Changes page first, or use git in TFN).

Cheat sheet: ./bin/tfn-studio doctor → ./bin/tfn-studio --tfn PATH serve --open → build → Stage → Changes → Apply → build module → restart server → test.

18. Using the studio with any module (nwn-manager)#

The studio is part of nwn-manager (studio/ in that repository). Besides The Frozen North it works on any module project that nwn-manager manages, including a brand-new one. The studio tells the two apart by itself:

Frozen North ("tfn" profile)Any other module ("generic" profile)
Folder layoutsrc/<type>/<resref>.<type>.json (nasher, one folder per type)nwn-manager project: everything side by side in unpacked/ (flat)
Quest scriptsTFN's own (inc_quest, dlg_q_*, ai_ondeath, area_init)the studio installs a small set of its own (below)
Quest Builderall features, Older/Modern script styleall features, Modern style only
Camp Builderplain and random campsplain camps (props and fixed creatures)
Spawn Designeryesnot shown (needs TFN's spawn engine)
Staging area, undo lognext to the studio (studio/.studio/)inside the project (.studio/, git-ignored)
Your quest/camp draftsstudio/specs/inside the project (studio-specs/, commit them)

18.1 Quick start on a module project#

cd ~/GIT/my_module                      # a project made by `nwn-manager init`
nwn-manager studio doctor               # checks the project, tools and NWN install
nwn-manager studio                      # the web UI for THIS project (http://127.0.0.1:8350)

Design a quest in Quest Builder, press Stage changes, review it on Changes, Apply, then nwn-manager repack to build the .mod. Everything else in this manual (sections 5-11) applies unchanged; the studio finds the project from the folder you are in (the nearest nasher.cfg), or from --module PATH / $MODULE_ROOT.

The same commands work without the web UI: nwn-manager studio quest stage <tag>, studio changes list|show|apply|undo, studio setup.

18.2 What the first quest installs#

A module such as Frozen North already has the scripts quests need. A fresh module has none, so the first quest you stage also stages the studio's quest runtime into the same change set (you can see it on the Changes page, and install it alone with nwn-manager studio setup; setup --check only reports):

File (in unpacked/)What it does, in plain words
inc_quest.nssThe quest "brain". Reads the notes on an NPC/creature/item/area (quest1, quest2, …), checks whether a player may take the next stage, records progress, and gives the reward.
dlg_q_adv.nss, dlg_q_chk_eli.nss, dlg_q_chk_atp.nss, dlg_q_chk_at.nssSmall dialog scripts. Each one is told which slot to look at through a dialog parameter (target = 3), so four scripts serve every quest (see 9.3).
enter_quest_adv.nssRuns when a player enters an area; advances "enter an area" stages. The area's OnEnter script is set to it.
qs_ondeath.nssCreature OnDeath script: credits a "kill" stage to the killer's whole party, then runs the standard death script. Set on kill targets whose death script is empty or the standard one.
qs_acquire.nssModule OnAcquireItem script for "pick up an item" stages. The studio sets it in module.ifo when that slot is empty; otherwise it tells you what to add to your own script.
qs_npc.utc.json, qs_questitem.uti.jsonPlain template NPC and item to clone quest NPCs and quest items from, so a module with no creatures yet can still make a quest giver.

How a player's progress is kept: as a whole number on the player character named after the quest (so it is saved with the character), plus the normal journal entry. Quest NPCs, kill targets, items and areas carry the same questK = "NN_<tag>" notes as in Frozen North, so everything in sections 9.1-9.4 holds (19 slots per object, 99 stages per quest, tags up to 27 characters).

The XP rule of this runtime is tier base (50/100/200/400) x level / 5, never less than the base. Edit AdvanceQuest in unpacked/inc_quest.nss to change it.

The studio never overwrites a script of yours: if the module already has a script with one of these names that is not the studio's, the quest is refused with a message that names it. Rename yours, or write the quest scripts by hand.

18.3 What is not available in a generic module#

  • Spawn groups, markers and random camps (Spawn Designer, the Random camp panel, encounter blueprints): they need Frozen North's own spawn engine (area_init). The studio refuses them with a clear message instead of writing files that would do nothing.
  • The Older script style and quest convert: the numbered scripts exist only in Frozen North.
  • Repeatable bounties (b_ tags): the generic runtime treats them like other quests (finish once).
  • Base-game creatures as templates: clone from your own module's creatures, or from the template NPC qs_npc. (Extracting base-game blueprints needs nwn_resman_extract, which is not bundled for macOS.)
  • The runtime needs NWN:EE (it uses GetScriptParam).

18.4 Notes for nwn-manager users#

  • nwn-manager init now git-ignores .studio/. For an existing project add the line /.studio/ to its .gitignore yourself.
  • The studio uses the tools nwn-manager already bundles (nwn_gff, nwnsc, nasher, the base-game scripts); nothing extra to install.
  • nwn-manager studio runs the studio from source with python3. A compiled nwn-pytools built before the studio existed does not know the command, so it is skipped for this subcommand until the binary is rebuilt (build/nwn-pytools.spec now bundles the studio).
